by: session, after Adrian's fourth watch (16 Oct 2026): the 2 flies into the power; compare, the insides fly out; each board carries the last line; 'negative one'; log3(-9) -> 3^? = -9 with the 3 and -9 moving as spoken

beats.say: Solve log base three of X minus eight equals two minus log base three of X.
asks: What does log base 3 mean?

beats.say: Here is the plan: get one log on each side, with the same base three.
asks: Why one log on each side?

beats.say: Then the logs match, so what is inside must be equal: square equals triangle.
asks: Why can we compare the insides?

beats.say: First, move minus log base three of X across. Crossing the equals sign, it becomes plus log base three of X.
asks: Why does the minus become plus?

beats.say: Now the two on the right. To match the plan, the two must become a log with base three.
asks: Why must 2 become a log?

beats.say: So two is two times one, which is two times log base three of three.
asks: Why is 2 = 2 log base 3 of 3?

beats.say: Log base three of three is one, because three to the power one is three.
asks: Why is log base 3 of 3 equal to 1?

beats.say: Now bring the two up into the power. Watch it move.
asks: Why can the 2 go up as a power?

beats.say: Two log base three of three is log base three of three squared. That is Bring down power, used backwards.
asks: What is Bring down power?

beats.say: Three squared is nine. So the two on the right is log base three of nine.
asks: Why is 2 = log base 3 of 9?

do.on: is log base three of nine

beats.say: Put log base three of nine in place of the two.
asks: Where did log base 3 of 9 come from?

beats.say: Now join the two logs on the left with Add Power.
asks: What is Add Power?

beats.say: In the law, M is X minus eight, and N is X.
asks: Which part is M and which is N?

beats.say: Adding logs multiplies the insides: log base three of X times X minus eight equals log base three of nine.
asks: Why is it x times x minus 8?

do.on: log base three of X times

beats.say: Now both sides are equal, and both are log base three. One log on each side, just like the plan.
asks: Why does the same base matter?

beats.say: So compare: what is inside the left log equals what is inside the right log.
asks: Why can we drop the logs?

beats.say: X times X minus eight equals nine.
asks: Why is x(x−8) = 9?

beats.say: We carry on from X times X minus eight equals nine.
asks: Where did this line come from?

beats.say: Expand: X times X is X squared, and X times minus eight is minus eight X.
asks: How do I expand x(x−8)?

beats.say: Bring nine across to make zero on the right. X squared minus eight X minus nine equals zero.
asks: Why make it equal zero?

do.on: X squared minus eight X minus nine

beats.say: Factorise: X minus nine, times X plus one, equals zero.
asks: How do I factorise this?

beats.say: So X equals nine, or X equals negative one.
asks: Why are there two answers?

beats.say: Now check each answer in the question. Start with X equals negative one.
asks: Why must I check the answers?

beats.say: Put X equals negative one into log base three of X minus eight.
asks: How do I put x = −1 in?

beats.say: Negative one minus eight is negative nine. So we get log base three of negative nine.
asks: Why negative nine?

do.on: log base three of negative nine

beats.say: This log asks a question: three, to what power, gives negative nine.
asks: What does log base 3 of −9 ask?

beats.say: Try some powers of three. Three to the one is three. Three to the zero is one.
asks: What is 3 to the power 0?

beats.say: Three to the negative one is a third. Three to the negative two is a ninth.
asks: Why is 3 to the −1 a third?

beats.say: Every power of three is positive. None of them gives negative nine.
asks: Why is every power of 3 positive?

do.text: all positive: no power of $3$ is $-9$

beats.say: So log base three of negative nine does not exist, and we reject X equals negative one.
asks: What does reject mean?

beats.say: X equals nine keeps both insides positive. The answer is X equals nine.
asks: How do I check x = 9?
